content.text:
Work item #1871 is done and converged.

**PR #2060** — *Delete the simulator's model: every scenario drives the real queue*, left open for review.

`test/sim/sim.mjs` was a second implementation of the dispatch mechanism beside `queue/`. It is now the wiring between the fake world H1 built and the real entry points — `schedulerRun`, `runExecutor`, `sweepQueue`, `continueOrEscalate`, `convergeOps`, the precondition engine and the anchor arithmetic are imported and run. 1481 lines of model became 838 lines of wiring; all 81 scenarios (every old title kept) drive the engine.

**Exit reads**: no `schedulerRun`/`janitor(`/`pickable(`/`claim(`/anchor arithmetic left in `sim.mjs`; every scenario green; the claim guard green both ways; whole suite 3585 tests / 0 failures; `check_the_world` 0 blocking, `check_the_work` clean.

**What driving the real code found** — four model/code disagreements, three of them the code:

1. An executor converged an item it had been reclaimed off. Without a heartbeat, S31b doesn't livelock as `PRINCIPLES.md` claimed — it double-executes, and the reclaimed-but-alive runner closes the item while its replacement is mid-work. Fixed: re-verify the claim after the work step.
2. A session's park left no episode boundary, so the next claimant lost forever to a dead claim — F18 through the one converge with no way to say it had let go. Fixed in `convergeOps`.
3. Queue membership was gated on the mark, a label the requester can remove — an adopted item then dropped out of every read at once. Fixed by accepting either artifact adoption wrote.
4. S41's claim was wrong, not the code (#1452 deliberately retired marker-routed parks). Claim corrected; three smaller ones too (S48, S65, S77).

Two things the link assumed were already there had to be built: a `run(world, …)` entry point for the scheduler run (H1's brief recorded it as landed; it wasn't), and a clock/timer a harness can install.

**One thing I changed from the spec, flagged for your call**: the 5-second budget for the whole `test/sim/` set was written against a model that made no API calls. The real engine costs ~3 ms per scheduler tick, so the set is ~13 s. The speed claim is stated per scenario instead (S80). If you want the 5 s figure kept, the route is fewer long-window scenarios, not a faster harness.

Exit reads and every decision are commented on #1869; #1871 is parked `needs-human-approval` with `Ends-when: #2060 closed`, so it ends by itself when you merge or close the PR. I've subscribed to the PR's activity — no checks have started on the head yet.

{"number":2060,"title":"Delete the simulator's model: every scenario drives the real queue (H2 of #1869)","body":"Link **H2** of #1869. `Refs #1869` — this advances the plan, it does not close it.

## What this does

`packs/claudinite-tasks/test/sim/sim.mjs` was a second implementation of the
dispatch mechanism beside `queue/`: its own scheduler run, its own pick order, its
own claim arbitration, its own anchor arithmetic, its own janitor. This deletes
that model. `sim.mjs` is now the wiring between the fake world H1 (#1347) built
and the real entry points — `schedulerRun`, `runExecutor`, `sweepQueue`,
`continueOrEscalate`, `convergeOps`, the precondition engine and the anchor
arithmetic are imported and run, and every one of the 81 scenarios drives them.

**Exit reads, on this branch:**

- `sim.mjs` contains no `schedulerRun` implementation, no `janitor(`, no
  `pickable(`, no `claim(` and no anchor arithmetic of its own — 1481 lines of
  model became 838 lines of wiring.
- every scenario green (81 titles, all the old ones kept), the claim guard green
  both ways, `check_the_world` 0 blocking, `check_the_work` clean, the whole suite
  green: **3585 tests, 0 failures**.

## What it found

The link says a disagreement between the model and the code is the finding, and
that the code being wrong makes the fix part of the change. Four disagreements;
three of them were the code.

**1. An executor converges an item it was reclaimed off.**
`src/execute/loop.mjs` re-verified nothing after the work step. The work step is
the one phase that may legally outlive the executing leash, and the beat that
keeps a live holder out of the reclaim is fail-soft by design — a partitioned
runner keeps working while its beats fail to post. Driven for real, S31b does not
livelock as `PRINCIPLES.md` claimed: it double-executes, and at minute 130 the
zombie closes the item `done` while its replacement is forty minutes into the same
work. Re-entrant code-work makes the second RUN safe and says nothing about a
second CONVERGE. Fixed: the stale runner re-verifies its claim and abandons
silently.

**2. A session's park leaves no episode boundary.**
A departing executor strikes its own claim; a session cannot — the claim is the
executor's and a session has no edit for it. So every claim of the parked episode
outlived the park, and the next executor to claim the re-queued item lost the race
to a dead claim, on its first try and on every try after it. That is F18 reached
through the one converge that had no way to say it had let go; S49 walks straight
into it. Fixed: the boundary rides the converge comment, a marker `claimWinner`
already reads whatever wrote it.

**3. Queue membership is gated on a label the requester can remove.**
`isQueueItem` counted an adopted marked issue only while it wore the mark. A
requester who takes their own label off drops the item out of every read of the
queue at once — never picked, never declined, and invisible to the janitor's
rules, which cannot sweep what they cannot list. S48's premise found it. Fixed by
widening to either artifact adoption wrote, which is the same "three signals, any
one sufficient" shape `converge-item`'s own refusal already took, for the same
reason (missingbulb/Shepherd#360).

**4. `S41` — the claim was wrong, not the code.**
`PRINCIPLES.md` said a worker naming its failure kind parks there. #1452
deliberately retired that: a failed run parks `failure` whatever the worker asked
for, because a worker naming `action` put a failed run in a non-blocking lane and
the task re-filed the next morning against a cause nobody had fixed. The verdict
now reaches the person in the park's comment. The claim is corrected; the
scenario asserts both halves.

Three more corrections of the same kind, smaller: S48 (the sanctioned withdrawal
is the mark **and** the status, as adoption's own comment instructs), S65 (there
is no close-time drain — the engine's only dispatch sites are the scheduler's
drain job and the failure continuation, so the chain's tail waits for the next
tick), and S77 (`create-work-item` stamps `Woken:` on every item it makes; what it
*refuses*, and so what nothing stamps, is an unqualified item of a scheduled task).

## The speed claim, restated

The link asked for 5 s over the whole `test/sim/` set. That figure was set against
a model that made no API calls. Driving the real engine costs about 3 ms per
scheduler tick, so `S21` alone — five quiet weeks, 859 ticks — is 2.6 s and the set
is ~13 s. The claim is stated per scenario instead, where it holds and where a
wall-clock wait creeping in actually shows up: **S80** asserts that a simulated
working day costs milliseconds and waits for nothing. Restating the budget is the
one place this PR changes what the link asked for, and it is stated here so it can
be overruled.

## Why this parks for review

The link authorizes `under:packs/claudinite-tasks/test; under:packs/claudinite-tasks/docs`.
This diff reaches outside it, deliberately and on the link's own instruction that a
fix to the code is part of the change:

| Outside the policy | Why |
|---|---|
| `src/schedule/run.mjs`, `src/world/clock.mjs`, `src/items/heartbeat.mjs`, `src/execute/loop.mjs` (seams) | H1's brief said phase 2 gave the shells `runExecutor`'s injectable shape; it did not, for the scheduler run. Without these three seams there is nothing to drive. No behaviour moves. |
| `src/execute/loop.mjs`, `src/items/work-item.mjs`, `src/session/converge-item.mjs` (fixes) | findings 1–3 above — behaviour changes, in the modules every member runs |
| `.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/workRules/consumer-safe-change.mjs` | the rule reported rewriting a test helper as a fleet migration; narrowed to the vendor set's own `TEST_DIR` |

So it is one PR under the policy, and the policy failing is the speed bump that
puts a person back on the trail rather than an error to route around.

## The diff is wider than the ask

Six folders: `src/schedule/`, `src/execute/`, `src/items/`, `src/session/`,
`src/world/`, `test/sim/`, plus `docs/` and one local-pack rule. The abstraction
that would have kept it in one place is the one H1's brief named and did not
land — a `run(world, …)` entry point per stage. Three of the four stages already
had one; the scheduler run did not, and giving it one is most of the non-test
diff. The three correctness fixes are each in a different module because the
three failures are: that is what deleting a model buys, and it is not something
an abstraction could have collected.

13	// deterministic and a scenario spanning a fortnight costs microseconds.

15	// ORDERING IS TOTAL: strictly by instant, FIFO within a tie. Two events booked
16	// for the same instant fire in the order they were booked, which is what lets a

26	  let t = at_(start);
27	  let seq = 0;
28	  const queue = [];

31	    now: () => new Date(t),
32	    nowMs: () => t,

37	  // current one rather than dropped: a fake that silently "missed" it would be
38	  // modelling a platform behaviour nobody asked for.
39	  const at = (when, fn) => { queue.push({ t: Math.max(at_(when), t), seq: seq++, fn }); return harness; };

43	  // beyond it SURVIVE for a later segment — a scenario runs in phases to assert
44	  // a mid-state, and a queue emptied at each boundary would lose them.
45	  //

47	  // a synchronous drain would let the next instant's event run while the last

49	  // exactly where a scenario is asserting an ordering.

12	// `updated_at` (#924). Any comment moves `updated_at` — including one written by
13	// an executor that LOST the claim race and let go — so a clock read off the issue
14	// defers the reclaim of an item nobody is working on. The struck claims a lost
15	// race leaves behind carry the episode marker, and are excluded here for exactly
16	// that reason.
17	
18	import { nowMs } from '../world/clock.mjs';
19	
20	import {
21	  CLAIM_MARKER, EPISODE_MARKER, PROGRESS_HEADING, parseProgressLines, withSection,
22	} from './work-item.mjs';
23	
24	export const HEARTBEAT_MARKER = '<!-- claudinite-heartbeat -->';
25	
26	// Comfortably inside the executing leash (60m), so a live holder is never
27	// reclaimed on a single missed beat: it takes four in a row.
28	export const HEARTBEAT_MS = 15 * 60e3;
29	
30	export const heartbeatComment = ({ executor, at, minutes }) =>
31	  `${HEARTBEAT_MARKER}\nStill working: executor \`${executor}\`, ${minutes} minute(s) in, at ${at}.`;
32	
33	// When the current holder last said anything — the newest live claim or heartbeat.
34	// A struck comment is not a signal: it says its author let the item go.
35	export function lastLivenessAt(comments = []) {
36	  const live = comments.filter((c) => {
37	    const body = c.body ?? '';
38	    if (body.includes(EPISODE_MARKER)) return false;
39	    return body.includes(CLAIM_MARKER) || body.includes(HEARTBEAT_MARKER);
40	  });
41	  const times = live.map((c) => new Date(c.created_at ?? 0).getTime()).filter((t) => t > 0);
42	  return times.length ? new Date(Math.max(...times)).toISOString() : null;
43	}
44	
45	// The timer the beat hangs on. A seam for the same reason the clock beside it is
46	// one: a harness that runs a work step in virtual minutes has no wall clock for a
47	// real interval to fire against, so the beats would be missing from exactly the
48	// timeline the executing leash is reading.
49	export const realTimers = Object.freeze({
50	  setInterval: (fn, ms) => setInterval(fn, ms),
51	  clearInterval: (id) => clearInterval(id),
52	});
53	
54	// Run `work` while beating. The beat is FAIL-SOFT — a comment that does not post
55	// must never sink a run that is otherwise fine — but never silent: a run whose
56	// heartbeat failed is one the leash may reclaim underneath it, and the log line is
57	// the only way to tell that from a run that simply finished quickly.
58	export async function withHeartbeat(work, { beat, intervalMs = HEARTBEAT_MS, log = () => {}, timers = realTimers }) {
59	  if (!beat || !(intervalMs > 0)) return work();
60	  const startedAt = nowMs();
61	  let beats = 0;
62	  const timer = timers.setInterval(() => {
63	    const minutes = Math.round((nowMs() - startedAt) / 60e3);
64	    Promise.resolve()
65	      .then(() => beat(minutes))
66	      .then(() => { beats += 1; })
67	      .catch((e) => log(`! heartbeat ${beats + 1} did not post (${e?.message ?? e}) — the leash may reclaim this item mid-work`));
68	  }, intervalMs);
69	  // `unref` so a beat pending at exit cannot hold the process open past its work.
70	  timer?.unref?.();
71	  try {
72	    return await work();
73	  } finally {
74	    timers.clearInterval(timer);
75	    const minutes = Math.round((nowMs() - startedAt) / 60e3);
76	    if (beats) log(`- work step ran ${minutes} minute(s) and beat ${beats} time(s)`);
77	  }
78	}
79	
80	// --- the agent phase's beat -----------------------------------------------------
81	
82	// The executor's beat above stops at the hand-off: its process exits, and an agent
83	// session then holds the item for as long as its own work takes. Nothing beat there,
84	// so the agent leash had only the issue's `updated_at` to read — the very clock this
85	// file exists to stop trusting.
86	//
87	// The session cannot beat the way the executor does. It has no process of its own to
88	// hang a timer on, and a scheduled wake reaches it between tool results rather than
89	// during one, so a beat that must fire inside a long call cannot be promised. What it
90	// can promise is a beat at each checkpoint its own work already has. Hence the
91	// interval below is a CEILING the session is asked to stay under, not a timer.
92	export const AGENT_BEAT_MS = 45 * 60e3;
93	
94	// Carries the same marker as the executor's beat, so `lastLivenessAt` counts an agent
95	// beat as the holder's own signal without knowing which phase wrote it.
96	export const agentBeatComment = ({ session, at, note }) =>
97	  `${HEARTBEAT_MARKER}\nStill working${session ? `: ${session}` : ''} — ${note}, at ${at}.`;
98	
99	// One progress line, appended to the item body's own `### Progress` section.
100	//
101	// APPENDED, not replaced: the body is the only surface a run can grow in place,
102	// because the GitHub toolset a session has offers comment creation and no comment
103	// edit. So the body carries the account and the beats carry the trail — the same
104	// split the standing trackers use, arrived at from the opposite direction.
105	export const withProgress = (body, line) =>
106	  withSection(body, PROGRESS_HEADING, [...parseProgressLines(body), line]);
107	
108	// WHEN THE WORK LAST MOVED, as distinct from when the holder last spoke.
109	//
110	// A beat resets the leash, so a session that beats punctually while wedged would
111	// never be reclaimed — the signal degrades from "work is happening" to "a process is
112	// alive", which is the failure the leash exists to catch. The beat already carries
113	// what separates them: its note is the progress (`9/15 groups triaged`), so a run of
114	// beats all saying the same thing is a wedged run, however punctual.
115	//
116	// Returns when the note last CHANGED — the oldest beat of the trailing run that all
117	// carry the newest one's note — or null when the item has no beats at all, which is
118	// the caller's signal to judge it the old way rather than to call it dead.
119	export function lastProgressAt(comments = []) {
120	  const beats = comments
121	    .filter((c) => (c.body ?? '').includes(HEARTBEAT_MARKER) && !(c.body ?? '').includes(EPISODE_MARKER))
122	    .map((c) => ({ at: new Date(c.created_at ?? 0).getTime(), note: beatNote(c.body ?? '') }))
123	    .filter((b) => b.at > 0)
124	    .sort((a, b) => a.at - b.at);
125	  if (!beats.length) return null;
126	  const newest = beats[beats.length - 1].note;
127	  let i = beats.length - 1;
128	  while (i > 0 && beats[i - 1].note === newest) i -= 1;
129	  return new Date(beats[i].at).toISOString();
130	}
131	
132	// The part of a beat that says where the work got to. Read off the comment rather
133	// than kept beside it: the beat a session posts through its own GitHub tools is the
134	// only copy, so the note has to survive the round trip through the rendered body.
135	const beatNote = (body) => {
136	  const line = body.split('\n').find((l) => l.startsWith('Still working')) ?? '';
137	  return (line.match(/ — (.*), at [^,]*\.$/)?.[1] ?? line).trim();
138	};
139

2	// is: it makes a run's answer depend on something outside its inputs. Every
3	// module under `src/` that needs the current instant asks here, so a simulator
4	// can drive a whole run at a chosen instant by replacing this one implementation
5	// and nothing else changes hands.
6	//
7	// Parsing a timestamp is NOT a clock read — `new Date(iso)` over a string a
8	// caller supplied is arithmetic, stays where it is used, and is deliberately
9	// outside what this port covers.
10	
11	// What "now" currently reads from. The wall clock in production, and whatever a
12	// simulator installed while it is driving a run.
13	let readMs = () => Date.now();
14	
15	// The current instant, as a Date. The one place `new Date()` is called with no
16	// argument anywhere under `src/`.
17	export const now = () => new Date(readMs());
18	
19	// The current instant in epoch milliseconds — for durations and unique suffixes,
20	// where a Date object would only be unwrapped again.
21	export const nowMs = () => readMs();
22	
23	// The current instant as the ISO-8601 string the queue's records are written in.
24	export const nowIso = () => new Date(readMs()).toISOString();
25	
26	// Replace the reading, and return the undo. This is the "replacing this one
27	// implementation" the header promises: a harness running the engine against a
28	// virtual clock installs its own instant here, and every `src/` module that asks
29	// for the time — the claim comment's stamp, a `Woken:` field, a minted branch's
30	// date — answers in that world rather than in this year.
31	//
32	// Deliberately a whole-process switch rather than a threaded argument: the point
33	// of a port is that a caller says what it needs and not where it comes from, and
34	// threading an instant through every module that reads one would put the clock
35	// back into every signature this module exists to keep it out of. Production
36	// never calls it; the undo is what keeps one harness's instant out of the next.
37	export function installClock(read) {
38	  const previous = readMs;
39	  readMs = read;
40	  return () => { readMs = previous; };
41	}

# The scenario harness — the mechanism, executable

A discrete-event harness that runs the REAL queue against a fake world, so the
mechanism's claims run as tests instead of living only as prose. Owner request,
2026-08-13: *"add the 'at time x — y happens' to the tests, and then execute the
simulator — this will help us make the design more robust."*

It began as a model — a second implementation of the dispatch mechanism beside
`queue/` — and that model caught real spec bugs prose replay missed (**F13**,
the occurrence guard's missing closed-at half; **F14**, the stale rule that can
never see a stuck *blocked* item; **F31**, the board's go rows eating an
occurrence; **F32**, the stateless `due:` term reading an unpicked deduped twin
as this period's run). Once the design shipped, the model stopped running ahead
of the code and started drifting behind it, so the model was deleted and the
scenarios were pointed at the engine itself. The first pass of that port found
three more, this time in the CODE rather than in the spec: an executor that
converges an item it was reclaimed off, a session park that leaves no episode
boundary, and a queue membership test a requester can fail by taking their own
label off.

- [`sim.mjs`](sim.mjs) — the harness: the wiring between the fake world and the
  real entry points, plus the scenario DSL. It holds no answer of its own —
  `schedulerRun`, `runExecutor`, `sweepQueue`, `continueOrEscalate`,
  `convergeOps`, the precondition engine and the anchor arithmetic are imported
  and run. Its own header says what it owns.
- [`world/`](world/) — the fake world: one module per port under
  [`packs/claudinite-tasks/src/world/`](../../src/world), in memory, plus
  `agents.mjs` and `humans.mjs`, which stand in for no port because neither is
  an edge the engine calls. Each module's header says what it models and what
  it does not. [`world/parity.test.mjs`](world/parity.test.mjs) is what stops a
  fake drifting from the port it stands in for, and
  [`world/world.test.mjs`](world/world.test.mjs) proves the behaviours the fake
  OWNS — the orderings the clock guarantees, the GitHub limitations the
  mechanism is designed around, the shape of a session's life.
- [`scenarios.test.mjs`](scenarios.test.mjs) — the play-throughs, one per named
  scenario. Each schedules world events at instants
  (`sim.at('2026-08-12T09:03Z', …)`), runs the virtual clock across a window,
  and asserts on the issue store the engine wrote and on the harness's log of
  what it drove.
- [`coverage.test.mjs`](coverage.test.mjs) — the two-way guard between this
  suite and [`packs/claudinite-tasks/docs/PRINCIPLES.md`](../../docs/PRINCIPLES.md):
  every scenario here is cited by some claim there, and every test PRINCIPLES.md
  cites actually exists.

Run: `node --test packs/claudinite-tasks/test/sim/*.test.mjs
packs/claudinite-tasks/test/sim/world/*.test.mjs`. Naming a folder alone does
not work: `node --test <dir>` does not recurse into it, which is also why the
`world/` glob is spelled out beside the first.

## What a scenario states, and what it may not

A scenario's task is a DECLARATION, in the same fields a real one uses: a
cadence term, a `schedule_after`, whether it has a work step and how long that
step takes. Its `precondition` function stands for every other condition a real
declaration would name in terms of its own signals, and is loaded as a
task-local TERM — so the real precondition engine evaluates it, in the real
expression, in the real two passes.

**A scenario may not state an answer.** Whether the item is filed, who wins the
claim, which park it lands in and what the day cost are all read back off the
world afterwards. Where a scenario and the engine disagree, the disagreement is
the finding: decide it by the claim the scenario cites in `PRINCIPLES.md` —
either the code is wrong and the fix is the change, or the claim is wrong and
correcting it is. Never weaken a scenario to make it pass.

**Write the scenario first.** A design change starts as a new or edited scenario
here, run red against the unchanged engine; the engine change makes it true; and
`coverage.test.mjs` is what stops `docs/PRINCIPLES.md` drifting out of step with
either side. A retired scenario's test deletes with it — PRINCIPLES.md's guard
has nothing to say about a scenario that no longer exists, only about one that
exists uncited.

**Everything waits on virtual time.** The clock is the only source of "later":
a real timer never fires here, and a promise that resolves from outside the
clock's own accounting is invisible to the pump that advances it. A scenario
that needs real time is a scenario written wrong (`S80`).

1	// THE FAKE CLOCK — virtual time and the ordered event queue every other fake
2	// module schedules on.
3	//
4	// It stands in for `src/world/clock.mjs`, so `port` carries exactly that
5	// module's names and nothing else; everything a scenario drives the clock WITH
6	// hangs off the harness object beside it. That split is what lets the parity
7	// guard compare key sets — a port that also carried `runUntil` could never be
8	// compared against the real one — and it is the shape every module in this
9	// folder takes.
10	//
11	// Time moves only when an event fires or a scenario advances it. There is no
12	// wall clock here at all — no `setTimeout`, no `Date.now()` — so a run is
13	// deterministic and a scenario spanning a fortnight costs microseconds.
14	//
15	// ORDERING IS TOTAL: strictly by instant, FIFO within a tie. Two events booked
16	// for the same instant fire in the order they were booked, which is what lets a
17	// scenario WRITE a race rather than hope for one.
18	//
19	// AN EVENT MAY WAIT FOR A LATER ONE, which is why the loop below is a pump rather
20	// than `await ev.fn()` per event. The code this harness drives is straight-line
21	// async — an executor run awaits its work step, and that step takes virtual
22	// minutes — so an event awaited to completion would be waiting on an event the
23	// queue can no longer reach. Instead an event is STARTED, and the clock advances
24	// only once every started event has either finished or parked on `sleep`.
25	// `running` counts the started, `waiting` the parked, and equality is quiescence:
26	// nothing is mid-step, so the next instant is safe to fire.
27	//
28	// `sleep` is therefore the only legal way to wait for virtual time from inside an
29	// event. A real timer would never fire at all here, and a promise resolved from
30	// outside the accounting is invisible to the pump — which would call the world
31	// quiet while a run was still mid-step.
32	
33	const at_ = (when) => (typeof when === 'number' ? when : Date.parse(when));
34	
35	export const MINUTE = 60_000;
36	export const HOUR = 60 * MINUTE;
37	export const DAY = 24 * HOUR;
38	
39	// How many macrotask turns the pump spends waiting for quiescence before it calls
40	// the world wedged. Generous — a cold dynamic import takes a few — and finite,
41	// because the alternative to this error is a test that hangs with no output.
42	const SETTLE_TURNS = 5000;
43	
44	export function makeClock({ start = '2026-08-12T00:00:00Z' } = {}) {
45	  let t = at_(start);
46	  let seq = 0;
47	  const queue = [];
48	  let running = 0;
49	  let waiting = 0;
50	  const failures = [];
51	
52	  const port = {
53	    now: () => new Date(t),
54	    nowMs: () => t,
55	    nowIso: () => new Date(t).toISOString(),
56	    // The real port's escape hatch, which this one has no use for: installing a
57	    // reading of "now" into the clock that IS the reading changes nothing. It is
58	    // here so the two ports stay comparable, and so a caller holding either can
59	    // call it without asking which it holds.
60	    installClock: () => () => {},
61	  };
62	
63	  // Book `fn` at an absolute instant. An instant already past is booked at the
64	  // current one rather than dropped: a fake that silently "missed" it would be
65	  // modelling a platform behaviour nobody asked for.
66	  const at = (when, fn) => { queue.push({ t: Math.max(at_(when), t), seq: seq++, fn }); return harness; };
67	  const after = (deltaMs, fn) => at(t + deltaMs, fn);
68	
69	  // Wait `ms` of VIRTUAL time from inside a running event. The wait is declared to
70	  // the pump, so the clock knows this event is parked rather than mid-step, and it
71	  // resumes as an ordinary booked event — a sleeper takes its turn in the same
72	  // total order as everything else.
73	  const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => {
74	    waiting += 1;
75	    at(t + Math.max(0, ms), () => { waiting -= 1; resolve(); });
76	  });
77	
78	  // Wait for something that is not virtual time but cannot settle until it
79	  // advances — a queued workflow run waiting for the one holding its concurrency
80	  // group. Declared to the pump the same way `sleep` is, because the alternative
81	  // is a world that never reaches quiescence and so never advances the clock the
82	  // waiter is waiting for.
83	  const park = (promise) => {
84	    waiting += 1;
85	    return Promise.resolve(promise).then(
86	      (v) => { waiting -= 1; return v; },
87	      (e) => { waiting -= 1; throw e; },
88	    );
89	  };
90	
91	  // Start an event without waiting for it. A rejection is collected rather than
92	  // thrown here: it belongs to the scenario that ran the segment, not to whichever
93	  // instant happened to be current when it surfaced.
94	  const fire = (fn) => {
95	    running += 1;
96	    Promise.resolve().then(fn).then(
97	      () => { running -= 1; },
98	      (e) => { running -= 1; failures.push(e); },
99	    );
100	  };
101	
102	  // Let every started event run until it finishes or parks. One macrotask turn
103	  // drains the whole microtask chain behind it, so ordinary async code — a promise
104	  // chain, an awaited fake API call, a cached dynamic import — settles in a turn or
105	  // two; only virtual time takes more.
106	  // Quiescence is "no started event is mid-step", which is `running <= waiting`
107	  // rather than equality: a scenario may sleep or park from OUTSIDE any event —
108	  // starting a run by hand and letting its body take virtual minutes — and such a
109	  // waiter is parked without ever having been counted as running.
110	  const settle = async () => {
111	    for (let i = 0; i < SETTLE_TURNS; i += 1) {
112	      await new Promise((r) => setImmediate(r));
113	      if (running <= waiting) return;
114	    }
115	    throw new Error(`the fake world did not settle: ${running - waiting} event(s) are still mid-step`
116	      + ' — something is waiting on a promise that virtual time can never resolve');
117	  };
118	
119	  // Fire every event strictly before `to`, then park the clock AT `to`. Events
120	  // beyond it SURVIVE for a later segment — a scenario runs in phases to assert
121	  // a mid-state, and a queue emptied at each boundary would lose them.
122	  const runUntil = async (to) => {
123	    const end = at_(to);
124	    for (;;) {
125	      await settle();

skills.name: committing
skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/committing

# Committing

- **One concern per commit.** If two changes could each stand alone, split them; a message that
  wants numbered items is the split talking.
- **Reference the issue, when the change has one** — `Refs #n`, or `Fixes #n` / `Closes #n` where
  the commit finishes it. A change tracked by its PR alone references nothing.
- **A landed commit is revised by a new commit**, never a rewrite of that one.
- **Stage by name** — `git add <paths>` for the files this commit is about; `-a` sweeps in whatever
  else was in progress.

skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/writing-repo-scanning-checks

# Writing a check that scans the repo

- **Choosing the file set** — take it from `git ls-files` rather than a filesystem walk with
  paths to skip, and remember a brand-new file is untracked until you add it, so a green run
  isn't coverage of it.

- **Scanning for a forbidden token** — strip comments first so it matches code, not prose —
  string-aware, since a `//` inside a URL is not a comment. Reuse `stripComments` from
  [`engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs`](../../../../engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs);
  if the scan can't import it, inline the same pass and point a comment back at that source.
  Strip in **both** directions — a comment that documents or warns about the banned pattern is
  exactly where a naive check trips over its own reasoning, so a commented-out instance must not
  count as present either.

- **Proving the check silent** — run it against the repo's own **real** sources, not only a
  synthetic clean fixture — a fixture spelling the same gap the check has just keeps proving the
  matching, and only a real-tree run can disagree with you.

skills.name: writing-tests
skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/writing-tests

# Testing practices

A consuming repo's own test *mechanics* — runner, layout, which suites exist — are its own docs'; CI-trigger rules and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` workflow-recursion gotcha are [git-github-advanced](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md)'s.

- See a test fail before you trust it: write it red before the fix (green after), or break what it guards and watch it go red. A test that has never failed proves nothing. For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. See-it-fail there **must** be the second method — mutate the new guard (weaken it), watch the test bite, then restore it. Restore with `git checkout -- <file>` (or `git stash`) taken at the moment of mutating — never a `.bak` copy saved earlier, which predates whatever else you edited in between and silently discards that intervening work. If the mutation was **staged** (to make a check that scans `git diff --cached` fire), a bare `git checkout -- <file>` restores from the index — which now holds the mutation — so the "restore" is a no-op; use `git checkout HEAD -- <file>` (or `git reset` first).
- A mechanism meant to survive a retry, re-queue, or hand-off needs a test that calls it twice, not once. A suite of single-call tests stays green while the multi-call case corrupts state — the double-call is what a real retry, requeue, or hand-off actually does. When the mechanism arbitrates by identity (a claim, a lock), the second call must come from a **different actor**: a single actor retrying its own stale claim can't expose an identity-masked race, since it still recognizes its own claim as valid.
- A simulator of a stateful mechanism must advance state only where the real engine's code actually leaves a mark — never wherever the rule's stated description says a transition happens. A sim that fires on every event matching the rule's *intent* is correct by construction against that rule and blind to exactly the silent paths where the real implementation and the rule have quietly diverged — which is where a genuine bug usually lives. Read the real engine's code for what it *writes*, and model that.
- Before trusting a new transform/normalizer, run it over the *real existing corpus* it will process, not just hand-picked test inputs — the live data exposes edge cases your examples won't. Relatedly, prefer a generic structural rule over a hand-maintained list of special cases: the enumerated list needs per-instance upkeep and silently has gaps, while a rule keyed on structure (e.g. "a known registry label under any 2-letter ccTLD") covers the whole class at once. (3)
- A test that stubs the exact boundary where the bug lives can't catch that bug — it guards only the shape it asserts, not the runtime effect. Say what it can't catch.
- A test that dereferences a path inside a **read-only dependency tree someone else refreshes** — a vendored mount, a synced submodule, generated output from an upstream build — is a test whose fixture a stranger can delete: the day upstream retires that file the case fails `ENOENT` with nothing in your repo having changed. Assert against a path only when the test itself creates it; when a case genuinely needs an upstream file, read it **defensively** and skip with a stated reason if it is gone, so a retirement upstream reports as "no longer applicable" rather than as your repo being broken. Check what actually runs these cases too — a suite that the repo's own gate never invokes reports its breakage to whoever happens to look.
- **Never test that a value is set.** A test that reads a value someone declared — a config or manifest field (`assert.equal(task.expected_outcome, 'fresh_pr')`), an exported constant or default object (`assert.deepEqual(DEFAULTS, {…})`), a settings file naming a pack, a workflow's `run:` line, a frontmatter key — and asserts it is the literal it was set to restates the file under test in a second file. It can only fail when someone changes the value **on purpose**, so it catches no defect and instead taxes every deliberate change with a mirrored edit — and teaches that the value is load-bearing prose to be restated, which is how one setting ends up copied into a comment, a worker doc, a README table and a test, so flipping it becomes a five-file diff. The see-it-fail test exposes it: to make the assertion go red you must break the thing it asserts, which is not a bug. "It exists", "it has the right shape" and "it is one of these" are the same test in a looser coat. Test the **behaviour the value drives** instead: feed the real code the declared value and assert what the code does with it — a task declared `weekly` is planned once across a fourteen-day clock, a check declared over `**/*.mjs` fires on a fixture `.mjs` and stays silent on a `.md`, a default object yields the documented output when nothing overrides it. Where no code reads the value there is nothing to test; if a declaration genuinely must not change without deliberation, that is a review concern, not a test. What *does* earn an assertion on declared data is a claim spanning two artifacts that could drift independently: the doc a field *names* exists; every signal the code reads is declared; two implementations of the same list agree; a value the runtime constrains is inside its legal set — proven by running the constraint, not by re-listing the set.
- **Testing a task's precondition or declaration** — assert only the pack's own code: a
  task-local term's decisions, a worker's behaviour, or a composition it designed; a plain
  built-in term or a validated declaration is the scheduler's own mechanism, proved once by its
  own suite.
- Prefer a single shared double; but when a subsystem is faked by more than one (a minimal unit stub vs. a faithful harness that boots the real module), a new call into the faked surface must be taught to **every** double, or the untaught one breaks — and the faithful harness turns an unmodeled API into a confusing **far-away** failure (a DOM-snapshot pixel-diff, not a local error at the call site). After adding a call into a faked boundary, find every double of it and extend each.
- When one wire format, encoding, or algorithm is **implemented twice** — two languages, two tiers, a hand-rolled client encoder against the server's library — no compiler, type system, or single test run spans the two, so the only thing holding them together is a **shared vector set carried deliberately by both suites**: the same inputs and the same expected outputs, asserted independently on each side, including the boundary cases the two could plausibly round differently (a value exactly on a bisection midpoint, a tie, a truncation edge). A vector asserted on only one side is an input nobody ever compared — both suites stay green, in different languages under different runners, while the claim quietly stops covering it. So: touching *either* implementation re-runs *both* suites, and adding a vector adds it to both. Where the pairing is mechanical (the two vector lists must contain the same inputs), pin it with a check rather than a convention.
- A traceability/coverage gate that requires every spec item be *claimed* by some test of one fixed kind proves only that it's claimed, not that it's verified. When items differ in kind, the gate green-lights claims that kind can't check — a pixel snapshot "covers" a click's tab-opening it can never observe, or a state the case never renders (and can't, when the data can't reach it). Segment the gate by the verification each item needs (route behavior to a behavior test, rendering to a snapshot) rather than forcing every item onto one mechanism. (1)
- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). Thread the reference time through the code under test, defaulting to the real clock in production. When retrofitting such a rule into an existing fixture suite, pin the reference instant so existing fixtures land on the same side they were authored for — so only the cases that deliberately exercise the new rule change and the diff stays small and reviewable, rather than a sprawling baseline churn that buries the intended change.
- A round-trip test that asserts by comparing **serialized** forms (`JSON.stringify(decoded) === JSON.stringify(original)`) silently makes key *order* part of the contract: add a field at the top of the encoder's record and append it in the decoder's, and the round-trip fails on ordering alone — with a diff that reads like a data bug and sends you after a value that was correct all along. Deep-equal the parsed structures instead, so the test states what it means; keep serialized comparison only where byte-identity is genuinely the property under test, and say so in the test.
- A new **e2e / heavy-browser** test must go green at least twice in CI before merging — one green run doesn't rule out a flake. This applies only to that class (the real-Chrome `test/fullBrowserHeavyTests/` suites); the deterministic offline/unit/integration tests don't touch a live browser or network, so one green run is enough for them.
- A test that can only run remotely (e.g. CI-only) must diagnose itself: on failure, dump the observed state, not just an assertion. It must also be *hang-proof* — bound every `await` (a timeout race) and set a test-level timeout — so a failure fails fast with that diagnostic instead of burning the whole job's timeout. An unbounded await on something that never settles (e.g. a callback that silently never fires) turns a 5-second failure into a 20-minute hang, and each CI-only iteration already costs a full round-trip.
- Run a suite you know is slow as **its own command with an explicit timeout well above its measured runtime**, and do the dependency install as a *separate, earlier* call. An agent shell caps a command at a default (order of a couple of minutes) and pushes it to the background when it expires; the reflex is then to start the suite over, so one green result costs double the wall clock with two suites racing each other. Chaining setup in front of the suite is what usually pushes the pair past the cap. If a run does get backgrounded, wait on the one already running rather than launching a second.
- To test code that drives a real browser or other external runtime in CI, prefer a *self-authored hermetic input* (e.g. a `data:` URL whose own script reproduces the behavior) over hitting a live third-party target — the live target is non-deterministic and often bot-blocked from a CI/datacenter IP, so it flakes or can't run, while a self-authored input exercises the same engine deterministically. (2)
- Gate a fuzzy quality metric (a coverage %, not a binary pass) behind a high-watermark: refresh the artifact and ratchet the watermark up locally, keep CI read-only (assert against the committed baseline, never rewrite it), and re-baseline by hand only when a deliberate change legitimately moves it — a number that can only climb catches a silent regression without flapping on noise. When the population it covers can *grow* (e.g. new test cases), store the set the watermark was computed over and gate only over the cases shared with it, so a newly added item is excluded rather than dragging the aggregate below the bar; re-anchor the watermark when the set changes. (A single aggregate watermark can then be re-anchored over a regression bundled into the *same* change as a set change — store per-item bars if that must be caught.)
- For behavior a person must sign off on (a third-party integration, an extraction result), keep a layer of declarative, human-reviewed expectation files — distinct from the unit tests, which nobody reads for *intent* — and cover every behavior change with a minimal, representative case there (one behavior per case, no incidental complexity), since that case is what gets reviewed.
- When a snapshot/golden test fails because the output *legitimately* moved (the pixels or bytes changed for a real reason), don't quietly regenerate the baseline to go green — an unreviewed baseline change is an unreviewed behavior change. Surface the diff (committed **expected**, newly-rendered **actual**, highlighted **diff**) and get owner approval before re-baselining; until then keep the *reverted* baseline committed so the branch honestly shows the test red-pending — never commit the new baseline first.
- When a test asserts exact values extracted from a captured artifact (a cached page, a recorded response), record and commit the artifact *first*, then read the expected values off the committed file — don't hand-write the expectations from memory or a live view and hope they match. Guessing the value desyncs the test from the real fixture; reading it off the committed bytes can't.
- A test that maintains a committed artifact should regenerate it into the working tree deterministically (no timestamps, so an unchanged run yields no diff) and skip the write under CI — never shell out to git from a test. Commit the artifact through the normal review flow, like a snapshot.
- Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. A surface that is inline-styled SVG, or flexbox-only markup authored for it, renders **bit-exact** through a headless rasterizer (e.g. satori → SVG, resvg → PNG) driven by the shipped code, using **bundled** fonts, never system fonts, and a pinned locale — demand a **zero-pixel** diff there. But that rasterizer has no CSS engine and draws no native widgets: a full shipped page using CSS **grid**, custom properties (`var()`), `@media`, **emoji**, or **form controls** (a range slider, radio, `<select>`) is beyond it — screenshot that with a **headless browser** instead, and allow a *small* diff tolerance (browser antialiasing varies across machines, so it isn't bit-exact). Match the engine to the surface; never reshape the product to fit the rasterizer. (A rasterized popup golden works only because the popup was authored flexbox-only — the moment a surface needs grid/vars/widgets, it needs a browser.) Since the browser goldens aren't gate-able bit-exact and a runner may lack the browser, let those cases **self-skip** where it's absent so the deterministic cases still gate.
- Reproduce a reported golden-image flake with the harness's own pixel comparator, never a raw byte or file-hash compare: a byte-hash is strictly tighter than a zero-pixel-diff comparator (it also fails on identical pixels re-encoded differently), so it manufactures "reproductions" of a flake that never fails the real gate.
- To image-golden a surface your code **injects into a host page** (a control mounted into a third-party toolbar), render it against a **committed capture of the real host DOM with its computed styles flattened inline** — the deterministic rasterizer reads only inline styles, and the host's own stylesheet is not yours to ship. Mount it with the **shipped injector** (so the golden proves the placement, not a hand-placed copy), and name the model's boundary honestly: substituted icon-font glyphs, an approximated host chrome (a captured sample is spec, not folklore — the origin lesson of a supported-targets matrix).

skills.name: running-the-suite
skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/running-the-suite

# Running the suite

- **The whole suite is one command** — `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`. There is no test
  script; `ci.yml`'s array is not authoritative. A bash glob without `globstar` is the dangerous
  substitute — it reached 37 of 65 files and reported nothing wrong — while `node --test <dir>`
  fails outright, so only the glob leaves you believing a green run. (4)
- **Read a run's output from a file** — redirect one run and grep that file for the slice you need;
  never re-run the ~55s suite to re-slice unchanged output. (1)
- **`git add` a new test file before certifying a run green** — `git ls-files` excludes an unstaged
  file, so the run never executed it; the `untracked-test-file` finding at Stop says which. (2)
- **Iterating on a sweep across many files** — run only the test files the edit touches, plus
  `check_the_work`; spend the whole suite and `check_the_world` once, at the end. Both are
  whole-tree aggregates whose verdict cannot turn on one file. (3)

skills.name: searching-for-a-tool
skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/searching-for-a-tool

# Searching for a tool

- **A search that finds nothing** is evidence about your query, not about the environment: vary
  the query before concluding a capability is absent, and try the tool before telling the owner a
  step is theirs.
- **`select:` matches the fully-qualified name only** — `select:mcp__<server>__<tool>`, copied off
  the deferred-tools listing. A short name after `select:` returns "no matching tools" while the
  tool sits in the listing, so reach for it when you have the server, or to load several at once.
- **A bare short name is a keyword query, and resolves** — `get_teams` on its own returns the
  tool. It is the form to use when you know the name but not the server. (1)
- **A server whose whole roster the deferred-tools listing already names** is the one exception: one
  miss there is the answer, so read the roster rather than rephrase the query.

Where the pairing is mechanical (the two vector lists must contain the same inputs), pin it with a check rather than a convention.
- A traceability/coverage gate that requires every spec item be *claimed* by some test of one fixed kind proves only that it's claimed, not that it's verified. When items differ in kind, the gate green-lights claims that kind can't check — a pixel snapshot "covers" a click's tab-opening it can never observe, or a state the case never renders (and can't, when the data can't reach it). Segment the gate by the verification each item needs (route behavior to a behavior test, rendering to a snapshot) rather than forcing every item onto one mechanism. (1)
- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). Thread the reference time through the code under test, defaulting to the real clock in production. When retrofitting such a rule into an existing fixture suite, pin the reference instant so existing fixtures land on the same side they were authored for — so only the cases that deliberately exercise the new rule change and the diff stays small and reviewable, rather than a sprawling baseline churn that buries the intended change.
- A round-trip test that asserts by comparing **serialized** forms (`JSON.stringify(decoded) === JSON.stringify(original)`) silently makes key *order* part of the contract: add a field at the top of the encoder's record and append it in the decoder's, and the round-trip fails on ordering alone — with a diff that reads like a data bug and sends you after a value that was correct all along. Deep-equal the parsed structures instead, so the test states what it means; keep serialized comparison only where byte-identity is genuinely the property under test, and say so in the test.
- A new **e2e / heavy-browser** test must go green at least twice in CI before merging — one green run doesn't rule out a flake. This applies only to that class (the real-Chrome `test/fullBrowserHeavyTests/` suites); the deterministic offline/unit/integration tests don't touch a live browser or network, so one green run is enough for them.
- A test that can only run remotely (e.g. CI-only) must diagnose itself: on failure, dump the observed state, not just an assertion. It must also be *hang-proof* — bound every `await` (a timeout race) and set a test-level timeout — so a failure fails fast with that diagnostic instead of burning the whole job's timeout. An unbounded await on something that never settles (e.g. a callback that silently never fires) turns a 5-second failure into a 20-minute hang, and each CI-only iteration already costs a full round-trip.
- Run a suite you know is slow as **its own command with an explicit timeout well above its measured runtime**, and do the dependency install as a *separate, earlier* call. An agent shell caps a command at a default (order of a couple of minutes) and pushes it to the background when it expires; the reflex is then to start the suite over, so one green result costs double the wall clock with two suites racing each other. Chaining setup in front of the suite is what usually pushes the pair past the cap. If a run does get backgrounded, wait on the one already running rather than launching a second.
- To test code that drives a real browser or other external runtime in CI, prefer a *self-authored hermetic input* (e.g. a `data:` URL whose own script reproduces the behavior) over hitting a live third-party target — the live target is non-deterministic and often bot-blocked from a CI/datacenter IP, so it flakes or can't run, while a self-authored input exercises the same engine deterministically. (2)
- Gate a fuzzy quality metric (a coverage %, not a binary pass) behind a high-watermark: refresh the artifact and ratchet the watermark up locally, keep CI read-only (assert against the committed baseline, never rewrite it), and re-baseline by hand only when a deliberate change legitimately moves it — a number that can only climb catches a silent regression without flapping on noise. When the population it covers can *grow* (e.g. new test cases), store the set the watermark was computed over and gate only over the cases shared with it, so a newly added item is excluded rather than dragging the aggregate below the bar; re-anchor the watermark when the set changes. (A single aggregate watermark can then be re-anchored over a regression bundled into the *same* change as a set change — store per-item bars if that must be caught.)
- For behavior a person must sign off on (a third-party integration, an extraction result), keep a layer of declarative, human-reviewed expectation files — distinct from the unit tests, which nobody reads for *intent* — and cover every behavior change with a minimal, representative case there (one behavior per case, no incidental complexity), since that case is what gets reviewed.
- When a snapshot/golden test fails because the output *legitimately* moved (the pixels or bytes changed for a real reason), don't quietly regenerate the baseline to go green — an unreviewed baseline change is an unreviewed behavior change. Surface the diff (committed **expected**, newly-rendered **actual**, highlighted **diff**) and get owner approval before re-baselining; until then keep the *reverted* baseline committed so the branch honestly shows the test red-pending — never commit the new baseline first.
- When a test asserts exact values extracted from a captured artifact (a cached page, a recorded response), record and commit the artifact *first*, then read the expected values off the committed file — don't hand-write the expectations from memory or a live view and hope they match. Guessing the value desyncs the test from the real fixture; reading it off the committed bytes can't.
- A test that maintains a committed artifact should regenerate it into the working tree deterministically (no timestamps, so an unchanged run yields no diff) and skip the write under CI — never shell out to git from a test. Commit the artifact through the normal review flow, like a snapshot.
- Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. A surface that is inline-styled SVG, or flexbox-only markup authored for it, renders **bit-exact** through a headless rasterizer (e.g. satori → SVG, resvg → PNG) driven by the shipped code, using **bundled** fonts, never system fonts, and a pinned locale — demand a **zero-pixel** diff there. But that rasterizer has no CSS engine and draws no native widgets: a full shipped page using CSS **grid**, custom properties (`var()`), `@media`, **emoji**, or **form controls** (a range slider, radio, `<select>`) is beyond it — screenshot that with a **headless browser** instead, and allow a *small* diff tolerance (browser antialiasing varies across machines, so it isn't bit-exact). Match the engine to the surface; never reshape the product to fit the rasterizer. (A rasterized popup golden works only because the popup was authored flexbox-only — the moment a surface needs grid/vars/widgets, it needs a browser.) Since the browser goldens aren't gate-able bit-exact and a runner may lack the browser, let those cases **self-skip** where it's absent so the deterministic cases still gate.
- Reproduce a reported golden-image flake with the harness's own pixel comparator, never a raw byte or file-hash compare: a byte-hash is strictly tighter than a zero-pixel-diff comparator (it also fails on identical pixels re-encoded differently), so it manufactures "reproductions" of a flake that never fails the real gate.
- To image-golden a surface your code **injects into a host page** (a control mounted into a third-party toolbar), render it against a **committed capture of the real host DOM with its computed styles flattened inline** — the deterministic rasterizer reads only inline styles, and the host's own stylesheet is not yours to ship. Mount it with the **shipped injector** (so the golden proves the placement, not a hand-placed copy), and name the model's boundary honestly: substituted icon-font glyphs, an approximated host chrome (a captured sample is spec, not folklore — the origin lesson of a supported-targets matrix).

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.
